Overseas Asset Allocation 2026: A Complete Guide to Five Tools for Taiwan's Wealthy, and the Cape Town Case

13 min read Overseas Property

If you are planning an overseas allocation, you have probably met two opposite pieces of advice. One says Taiwan's investors do not need to go abroad at all, because the local stock market is enough. The other says the wealthy have already moved their money out, so what are you waiting for. Both are oversimplifications. What is worth looking at is what the data actually says - and a third route that few people consider but that operates very maturely in the Cape Town market: putting part of your portfolio into a physical-asset market whose correlation with US and Japanese equities is low.

Start with the facts. According to Financial Supervisory Commission statistics, by the end of June 2026 high-net-worth clients with more than NT$100 million in assets numbered 26,000, managing NT$2.8 trillion, with the market expecting the figure to pass NT$3 trillion before year-end. A CTBC Bank survey puts the number of NT-dollar billionaires at 123,000, and among the ultra-high-net-worth tier above NT$10 billion, the share holding overseas assets reaches 86%. A separate HSBC report, the 2026 Global Affluent Investor Snapshot, shows Taiwan's affluent investors' overseas preference jumping 16 percentage points to 44%, with the most favoured markets being the United States (52%), mainland China (38%) and Japan (34%). South Africa and other emerging-market physical assets barely appear on that list at all.

Put those numbers together and a clear structure emerges: the overseas share of Taiwan's high-net-worth portfolios is rising fast, but the direction is highly concentrated. This article is not about whether to allocate overseas. It is about a more practical question - beyond the popular markets of the US and Japan, why Cape Town deserves a place on the same allocation table, and by what standard different overseas assets should be compared.

Key takeaways: Taiwan's high-net-worth overseas allocation is accelerating - 86% of the billionaire tier already holds assets abroad, and affluent investors' overseas preference has risen to 44%. But the mainstream direction is concentrated in the US and Japan, while physical assets in markets such as South Africa are relatively ignored. No allocation tool is inherently better than another; what matters is whether your objective is cash flow, capital growth or risk diversification. Cape Town property references a gross rental yield of roughly 5-8% (a market reference range; actual results depend on occupancy and tax, and are not guaranteed), and can be one piece in diversifying single-market and single-currency risk. This article is for information only and is not investment advice.

The overseas share held by high-net-worth clients is far above the average investor

What Is Overseas Asset Allocation, and Where Do Taiwan's Wealthy Actually Put Their Money?

Direct answer: overseas asset allocation means holding part of your assets in markets and currencies outside your home country in order to diversify single-market, single-currency and single-political risk - not simply to chase a higher return. Taiwan's high-net-worth investors currently run a high-equity, high-cash, low-physical-asset mix: equities are around 30% of the total (against a global average of only 16-17%), cash around 23%, and overseas preference has risen to 44% - but the actual vehicles for those overseas positions remain US equities, bonds and funds.

HSBC's 2026 survey paints a very concrete picture (Source: HSBC Global Affluent Investor Snapshot 2026): Taiwan's wealthy hold equities at 70%, far above the global average of 52%; equities account for about 30% of total asset allocation, nearly double the global average; and the cash share has fallen year by year from 33% in 2024 to 23% in 2026. Over the next twelve months, the top three planned additions are gold and precious metals (+19%), high-yield call accounts (+18%) and multi-asset managed solutions (+15%) - all three are liquid instruments, and none is registrable physical real estate such as South African or Cape Town property.

That mix reveals one thing: Taiwan's high-net-worth overseas allocation is in fact heavily concentrated in financial assets. Equities, funds, insurance policies, deposits and gold are all highly liquid vehicles that can be adjusted quickly. They solve market diversification and currency diversification, but they do not solve something else - and that is exactly where Cape Town property enters the high-net-worth allocation discussion:

when what you want is a long-hold physical asset with predictable cash flow, a financial instrument is not necessarily the right container.

That is why Cape Town property is rarely mentioned in allocation discussions yet deserves a place on the comparison table. It is not meant to replace US equities or overseas bonds; it fills the position of "non-US, non-Asian, priced in physical assets, and able to generate rental cash flow". For someone who already has more than 80% of their assets in financial instruments and Taiwan-dollar assets, that is a structurally different piece of the puzzle.

Before comparing tools, one point must be made clear:

the first principle of overseas allocation is not the rate of return, but why you want this position at all. If the answer is risk diversification, what you compare is correlation and holding costs; if the answer is cash flow, what you compare is net yield and management burden; if the answer is succession, what you compare is legal structure and tax efficiency. The three objectives lead to completely different choices - and Cape Town property will be judged completely differently under each of them.

Holding-cost structure, not headline yield, decides your net return

Which Tools Should You Compare - Property, Insurance, Brokerage, Deposits or Gold?

Direct answer: there is no "best tool", only the tool that best matches your objective. Overseas property suits those seeking physical assets and rental cash flow; an overseas insurance policy suits tax and succession planning; an overseas brokerage account suits liquidity and market growth; a foreign-currency deposit suits short-term parking and currency hedging; gold suits hedging systemic risk. The real standard is after-tax net return divided by the management burden you are willing to carry - not the headline yield. Cape Town property deserves separate discussion because its cost structure differs sharply from financial products.

ToolPrimary functionLiquidityManagement burdenReturn profile
Overseas property (e.g. Cape Town)Physical asset, rental cash flow, long-term appreciationLow (2-4 month transaction period)Medium (can be delegated to local property management)Rental income plus capital growth
Overseas insurance policyTax deferral, succession structure, asset isolationLow (early surrender is costly)LowPolicy value growth
Overseas brokerage accountMarket growth, equity and bond allocationHigh (trade any time)LowDividends plus capital gains
Foreign-currency depositShort-term parking, currency hedgingHigh (available at maturity)Very lowInterest
Gold / precious metalsSystemic risk hedgeHighLowPrice movement

For Taiwan's high-net-worth investors, the most common bias is comparing nominal yields only, without comparing holding costs or structural differences. Take overseas property: a rental unit in Cape Town may reference a gross rental yield of about 5-8% (a market reference range; actual results depend on occupancy and tax, and are not guaranteed), but what actually determines what you keep is tax, levies, property-management fees, vacancy and currency. The after-tax net cash flow left once those are deducted is the number that can sit on the same table as an overseas bond coupon or a deposit rate.

South Africa's holding-cost structure has two features that matter especially to overseas investors. First, rental income and holding expenses (including levies and some municipal charges) can be treated as operating expenses when you file, with the deductible scope determined by SARS rules and your tax residency status. Second, the title system follows English common law: foreigners can obtain full registrable title, and funds are delivered through an attorney's trust account - for buyers unfamiliar with South African law, that is the key mechanism that lowers transaction risk.

Three questions for choosing a tool: (1) Is this position for cash flow now, or appreciation in ten years? (2) How much management burden can I carry - monthly bills, annual filings, unexpected repairs? (3) If this market's currency, the rand for instance, falls 20% within five years, does my Cape Town allocation plan still hold? Only when you can answer all three is it worth discussing allocation size.

Currency is both the source of return and the source of risk in overseas allocation

How Should You Manage TWD-ZAR Currency Risk?

Direct answer: currency risk cannot be eliminated, only managed. There are three methods: (1) hold long term to average out entry and exit rates; (2) enter in tranches, dollar-cost-averaging style, rather than concentrating at a single point; (3) keep rental income in the local currency, reinvested locally or held in a local account, to reduce the friction cost of repeated conversions. At early-October 2026 rates, ZAR 1 equalled about NT$1.92, or about US$0.0605 (Source: ECB reference rates / open.er-api.com, 7 October 2026).

Currency plays a dual role in overseas allocation: it is both a source of return and a source of risk. The rand's historical volatility is greater than that of the Taiwan dollar or the US dollar, which means two things are true at once. When the rand is relatively weak, the same amount of Taiwan dollars buys more South African assets, creating a discount effect. But when you later repatriate rent or sale proceeds to Taiwan, currency moves will directly amplify or erode your real return.

The practical approach is to run a stress test first rather than forecast the exchange rate. Here is a concrete example. Assume you invest about R5 million in a Cape Town rental property (roughly NT$9.6 million). Ignoring tax and property-management costs for simplicity, and assuming a 6% gross annual rental yield (a market reference range), the impact of currency moves on total return when you sell five years later looks like this:

Rand scenario at saleZAR 1 in Taiwan dollarsImpact on repatriated amount (vs base case)
Rand depreciates 20%about NT$1.54Repatriated amount shrinks by about 20%
Rate unchangedabout NT$1.92Base case
Rand appreciates 20%about NT$2.30Repatriated amount increases by about 20%

The point of this table is not that the rand will rise, but that currency can swing the outcome of the same investment by a full 20% in either direction. Treating the South Africa position as a long-hold physical asset, and letting rent circulate locally, usually reduces decision pressure more than trading in and out hoping for currency gains. If the position is too large relative to your total assets, currency moves will dominate your overall return - in which case you should adjust the size first, not try to forecast the rate.

Another practical detail that is often overlooked is remittance and reporting. Cross-border transfers must comply with South Africa's foreign-exchange reporting rules (BOP reporting), and there are corresponding reporting obligations on the Taiwan side. In the Cape Town purchase process, for example, funds must first enter the local attorney's trust account and are released according to registration progress, so each remittance corresponds to a set of documents and a defined milestone. None of this is difficult, but it needs planning; understanding the process once is far easier than remedying paperwork later.

Sources: ECB reference rates / open.er-api.com (7 October 2026); SARB Exchange Control / BOP reporting rules. The scenario figures are set by the author using a market reference range and are not forecasts.

Succession structure must be planned at purchase, not repaired at inheritance

What Should Taiwan's Wealthy Families Watch in Cross-Border Succession of Overseas Property?

Direct answer: the key to cross-border succession is the holding structure at the time of purchase, not remediation when inheritance occurs. Holding overseas property directly in your own name subjects the inheritance process to the law and tax system of the country where the asset sits. Holding through a trust or company gives more flexibility but raises cost and complexity. For Cape Town property, foreign heirs will face South African estate duty and inheritance procedure, so structure should be settled before purchase.

South Africa's estate duty is currently 20%, with 25% applying to the portion above R30 million; the estate is calculated after deducting debts, funeral costs and the statutory abatement (Source: SARS Estate Duty; South African tax system 2026). In addition, South Africa applies the Intestate Succession Act's mandatory order of inheritance on intestacy, which differs from Taiwan's Civil Code order - so without prior arrangements, a cross-border inheritance can face two legal systems at once.

That sounds complicated, but in practice it breaks into three decisions:

1

Decide the holding name

Direct personal ownership is simplest with the most tax transparency, and most foreign buyers of Cape Town property take this route. A company or trust adds structural flexibility but brings annual filing and maintenance costs. The choice depends on whether you have cross-generational needs.

2

Arrange inheritance documents in advance

South African wills must meet local formal requirements. A Taiwan will dealing with South African assets may not be recognised by South African authorities, so prepare documents in both jurisdictions and confirm they cross-refer.

3

Assess the two-way tax interaction

Taiwan and South Africa define tax residency differently and tax estate and gift differently. The tax efficiency of a cross-border structure must be assessed jointly by professionals in both countries - consulting only one jurisdiction is not enough.

It is worth emphasising:

succession structure should not wait until assets reach a certain size. The moment you decide to add Cape Town property to your overseas allocation, the holding name should be decided at the same time - because changing structure later usually involves title transfer, tax and cost, and is far more expensive than choosing correctly at the start. That is where the advisory role in overseas allocation is genuinely valuable: not picking the property for you, but thinking the structure through before you buy.

Cape Town's physical-asset characteristics are something financial tools cannot replicate

Why Put Cape Town on the Overseas Allocation Comparison Table?

Direct answer: because Cape Town offers a combination other popular markets struggle to provide. (1) Geographic diversification that is neither US nor Asian. (2) Pricing in physical assets rather than another financial certificate. (3) Predictable rental cash flow. (4) A title system following English common law, under which foreigners can hold in full. (5) A discount effect when the currency is relatively weak. It is not meant to replace US equities or overseas bonds, but to fill the empty position in the allocation table labelled "emerging-market physical assets".

As noted earlier, Taiwan's high-net-worth overseas positions are heavily concentrated in the US (52%), mainland China (38%) and Japan (34%). Those three markets solve the problem of leaving the Taiwan dollar, but they also create a new concentration risk: if US-dollar assets and US equities already dominate your portfolio, putting more money into US-dollar assets only moves concentration from one market to another. Real diversification needs lower-correlation exposure - and Cape Town property's correlation with US and Taiwan equities sits at that lower end.

Cape Town property's structural features deserve item-by-item review. First, its demand does not come only from foreign investors: South Africa's domestic semigration flow continues into the Western Cape, forming a layer of local hard demand, which differs from markets that depend purely on foreign capital. Second, the South African Reserve Bank raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 7.25% on 23 September 2026, lifting the prime rate to 10.75% (Source: SARB, 23 September 2026); higher borrowing costs make the relative advantage of all-cash buyers clearer, and make negotiation room in tight premium segments more meaningful. Third, Cape Town's main residential types reference a gross rental yield of about 5-8% (a market reference range; actual results depend on occupancy and tax, and are not guaranteed), a cash-flow structure clearly different from Asian gateway cities with low rental yields.

Comparison dimensionCape Town propertyUS equities / overseas fundsForeign-currency deposit
Asset typePhysical real estate (registrable title)Financial certificateDeposit claim
Source of cash flowRent (can be delegated to local property management)Dividends / distributions (variable)Interest (fixed)
Correlation with Taiwan and US equitiesLowHighLow
LiquidityLow (2-4 month transaction period)HighHigh
Main risksCurrency, local legislation, vacancyMarket volatilityReal purchasing power eroded by inflation

The most honest part of that table is the liquidity row: Cape Town property is clearly less liquid than financial assets. That is not a weakness dressed up as a strength, but a trade-off you have to accept - lower liquidity buys lower market correlation and registrable physical title. If your asset structure is already highly liquid, say more than 80% in equities and cash, adding a block of illiquid physical asset can actually reduce overall portfolio volatility.

Finally, back to the question of proportion. In practice, start by asking yourself one question:

If this Cape Town property could not be sold at all for five years, would my life and other investment plans be affected?

If the answer is no, it fits a long-term core allocation. If the answer is yes, then no matter how attractive the yield, the proportion should be reduced. That is allocation discipline, and the only way to protect yourself from being tied to a single market.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is overseas asset allocation, and what share do Taiwan's wealthy hold abroad?

Overseas asset allocation means holding part of your assets in markets and currencies outside your home country to diversify single-market, single-currency and single-political risk. Taiwan's high-net-worth investors currently run a high-equity, high-cash, low-physical-asset mix: equities around 30% of the total, cash around 23%, and overseas preference up to 44%, while physical real estate such as Cape Town property has almost no position. A CTBC survey shows 86% overseas holdings among the billionaire tier. (Sources: HSBC Global Affluent Investor Snapshot 2026; CTBC survey; FSC statistics, June 2026.)

Why should Taiwan's overseas allocation not be limited to the US market?

Because leaving the Taiwan dollar is not the same as diversifying risk. The top three overseas preferences of Taiwan's affluent investors are the US (52%), mainland China (38%) and Japan (34%). If US-dollar assets already dominate your portfolio, adding more only moves concentration to another market. Real diversification needs lower-correlation exposure, such as a market priced in physical assets whose demand includes local domestic consumption - Cape Town qualifies, because its demand base includes Western Cape semigration as well as foreign investors. (Source: HSBC Global Affluent Investor Snapshot 2026.)

How do you choose between property, insurance, brokerage, deposits and gold?

Match the tool to the objective: physical assets and rental cash flow call for overseas property; tax deferral and succession structure call for an overseas policy; liquidity and market growth call for an overseas brokerage account; short-term parking and currency hedging call for a foreign-currency deposit; hedging systemic risk calls for gold. Cape Town property plays the physical-asset-plus-rental role and does not overlap with a policy or a brokerage account. The real standard is after-tax net return divided by the management burden you are willing to carry, not headline yield.

What gross rental yield does Cape Town property deliver?

Cape Town's main residential types reference a gross rental yield of about 5-8% (a market reference range; actual results depend on occupancy, tax and management costs, and are not guaranteed). Deduct municipal rates, levies, property-management fees, vacancy and currency effects, then compare after-tax net cash flow with other tools. Past performance does not indicate future returns.

How should TWD-ZAR currency risk be managed?

Currency risk cannot be eliminated, only managed: hold long term to average entry and exit rates; enter in tranches rather than in one position; and let rental income circulate locally to reduce repeated conversion costs. At early-October 2026 rates, ZAR 1 was about NT$1.92, or about US$0.0605. (Source: ECB reference rates / open.er-api.com, 7 October 2026.)

What legal misconceptions do Taiwanese buyers most often have about overseas property?

Three recur most often. First, that overseas property must be held through a company - in fact direct personal ownership is the simplest and most tax-transparent route, with company or trust structures used for cross-generational needs. Second, that a Taiwan will can deal with overseas assets - South African wills must meet local formal requirements, and documents should be prepared in both jurisdictions. Third, that paying the seller directly is fastest - South African law requires funds to sit in an attorney's trust account and be released only on completion of registration, which is precisely the buyer-protection mechanism. Tax efficiency of a cross-border structure should be assessed by professionals in both countries; this article is not legal or tax advice.

Why Handle This Through Crestline Advisory?

South African documentation requirements change every year — and what changes is usually the format, not the eligibility. Same passport, same proof of address, wrong format, rejection.

The three most common failure points

  • Passport certification rejected: A plain true-copy stamp is not accepted. A commissioner of oaths must certify in English, confirm the original was seen, add a true-likeness statement for photo pages, and include signature, date, address and occupation.
  • TIN left blank without a reason code: For Taiwanese clients the tax number is the national ID number. Leaving it blank requires ticking Reason A / B / C with an explanation.
  • Proof of address older than three months: Measured from the application date. Past the deadline the entire application is void and must be resubmitted.

Working through our partner Crestline Advisory (on-the-ground execution in South Africa) means these are checked before submission: document format pre-screened item by item (avoiding a 2-4 week round trip), current bank requirements confirmed before you book any flight, remittance routing and BOP declaration categories aligned in advance, and progress tracked locally after submission.

DingYao verifies your documents on the Taiwan side and hands over to Crestline Advisory for execution. You do not receive a checklist and left to figure it out alone.
